title: Reforming the Judiciary -- Ch. 5: Good Governance Begins with Ethics
keywords: I want to be a lawyer
censured one of its own members
primary_topics: Chapter 5 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' -- an address arguing that quality justice and good governance always begin with ethics, opened with a law student's column and a lawyer joke about the profession's bad press before turning to the hard survey evidence of perceived corruption in the bench and bar.

CJP answered the complaints against judges and lawyers with two assurances: that the vast majority are honest, competent, hardworking and God-fearing, and that the Supreme Court had instituted a wide-ranging reform program, the 'Davide Watch' and its Action Program for Judicial Reform, to address the problems.

He presented ethics as the central theme of that reform program, citing the Court's unprecedented disciplinary record -- censuring one of its own members, dismissing a Court of Appeals justice, suspending the presiding magistrate of the Sandiganbayan, and disrobing, fining or disciplining hundreds of lower-court judges.

He argued that discipline alone is not enough: the judiciary must also attract the best and the brightest, which requires rationalized judicial compensation through real fiscal independence and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, and which forbids funding arrangements that would compromise judicial independence.
sub_topics: Opening with Joan A. de Venecia's 'YoungBlood' column 'I want to be a lawyer' (Philippine Daily Inquirer, May 16, 2002), quoted on lawyers' bad press as 'guns for hire' and on the joke about ten thousand lawyers drowned in the sea being 'a good start.'
A second joke -- the lawyer who denied under oath kicking his wife on the ground that 'She is not my wife!' -- before he turns serious.

The evidence of perceived corruption: the World Bank report 'Combating Corruption in the Philippines' citing a February 2000 Social Weather Stations survey in which 62 percent believed there were significant levels of corruption in the judiciary, 65 percent that many or most lawyers could be bribed, and 57 percent the same of judges.
The other accusations hurled at judges and lawyers: deliberate delay, incompetence, arrogance, neglect of duty, conduct unbecoming, partiality and immorality.
Two assurances: that the vast majority of judges and lawyers are honest, competent, hardworking and God-fearing, and that the Supreme Court has firmly instituted a wide-ranging reform program.

The 'Davide Watch' announced on November 30, 1998, envisioning an independent, effective and efficient judiciary worthy of public trust and a legal profession giving quality, ethical, accessible and cost-effective legal services -- implemented day after day as the ongoing APJR and backed by the national government, local donors, UNDP, the World Bank, ADB, UNICEF, the Asia Foundation and bilateral aid from Japan, Canada, Australia, the United States and the Netherlands.

The breadth of the reforms: law school curricula, the bar examinations, financial aid for bright but poor law students, professorial chairs and endowments, rigid screening of appointees, strict enforcement of ethics, continuing legal education, and rigorous monitoring of judicial personnel.

Ethics as the central theme: increasingly strict enforcement of the Code of Judicial Conduct and the Code of Professional Responsibility, held to a stricter standard than RA 6713's Code of Conduct and Ethical Standards for public officials generally.

The disciplinary record: for the first time in its 100-year history the Court censured one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice and suspended the Sandiganbayan presiding magistrate from his administrative functions; since November 30, 1998 it had disrobed more than 20 lower court judges, fined more than a hundred and disciplined more than two hundred others.

Recruitment as the harder half of the problem: more than one third of all trial courts vacant because of low compensation and security concerns, with RTC judges paid P25,333, CA and Sandiganbayan magistrates P27,500 and Supreme Court justices P38,500 -- less than some secretaries and clerks in big Makati companies.

The two legislative fixes: real fiscal independence through a lump-sum appropriation of, say, two percent of the national budget for the Court itself to allocate, and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law so judicial officials can be paid properly without additional appropriation.

The shrinking budget: the judiciary's share fell from about two percent of the national budget in the early 90s to less than one percent in the current year, despite constitutional fiscal independence.

Objection to local government 'allowances' and 'expense reimbursements,' which are granted unevenly according to LGU capacity and official generosity and which breed suspicions of bias because mayors and governors have occasional court cases.
The declined corporate fundraising offer and the journalist's question about donor conditions, both answered by the principle that assistance must not compromise judicial independence.
The close: the four 'ins' of a good judge -- integrity, independence, intelligence and industry -- all encapsulated in ethical conduct.

stances.claim: Although there are some undesirable judges and lawyers, the vast majority are honest, competent, hardworking and God-fearing, and the complaints against the professions must be answered without conceding that the professions are corrupt.
stances.rhetorical_move: concede-then-bound: acknowledging the bad press and the survey numbers, then confining the fault to a minority before presenting the institutional remedy

stances.claim: Ethics is the central theme of the judicial reform program, and the Supreme Court has rightly chosen to enforce its own Code of Judicial Conduct and Code of Professional Responsibility even more strictly than the general ethical standards that RA 6713 imposes on all public officials.
stances.rhetorical_move: higher-standard argument, evidenced by an unprecedented disciplinary record -- a censured member of the Court, a dismissed Court of Appeals justice, a suspended Sandiganbayan presiding magistrate, and hundreds of disciplined lower-court judges

stances.claim: Weeding out the undesirables is not enough; the judiciary must attract and keep the best and the brightest, which cannot happen while more than a third of trial courts are vacant and judges earn less than clerks in big Makati companies -- so judicial compensation must be rationalized through real fiscal independence and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law.
stances.rhetorical_move: insufficiency-of-discipline pivot, backed by vacancy rates and exact salary figures and resolved into two named legislative asks

stances.claim: Funding must never be allowed to compromise judicial independence: he declined a business leader's offer to solicit one percent of the net profits of the top 1,000 companies, and he objects even to the allowances local government units give judges, because LGU officials have occasional court cases and the grants are uneven.
stances.rhetorical_move: refusal-by-example: declining a helpful offer in order to demonstrate the principle, and extending the same logic to an existing practice

notable_anecdotes: He opened by quoting Joan A. de Venecia, a 21-year-old UP law freshman, whose 'YoungBlood' column of May 16, 2002 recounted that lawyers are depicted as 'guns for hire' and that the famous answer to 'What do you call 10,000 lawyers drowned in the sea?' is 'a good start.'

He told the joke of the lawyer asked under oath whether he had kicked his wife, who insisted the accusation was absolutely false because 'She is not my wife!' -- then announced that he would now be serious.

Two years earlier, after he had spoken on the judiciary's financial problems at a Management Association of the Philippines meeting, a sympathetic business leader offered to ask the top 1,000 Philippine companies to donate one percent of their net profits to the judiciary, as they did for Philippine Business for Social Progress; CJP appreciated the intention but declined, saying it might compromise independence in labor, corporate or tax cases.

At an open forum at the Manila Overseas Press Club, a journalist asked whether accepting World Bank and ADB assistance would compromise the Court's independence given those agencies' policies of free trade and globalization; he answered that the assistance was really going to the national government, which would turn it over to the judiciary without conditions or 'strings attached.'

He noted that he had already discussed the progress of these pursuits in detail in three books written over the last three years, and could not expound on them all in the twelve minutes given him for the address.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 5 of 'Reforming the Judiciary' reproduced an address on ethics and good governance that opened lightly and turned grave. Justice Panganiban quoted Joan A. de Venecia, a 21-year-old UP College of Law freshman, whose 'YoungBlood' column of May 16, 2002 in the Philippine Daily Inquirer noted that lawyers are depicted as 'guns for hire' and that the standard answer to 'What do you call 10,000 lawyers drowned in the sea?' is 'a good start'; he added a joke about a lawyer who denied under oath kicking his wife because 'She is not my wife!' He then cited the World Bank report 'Combating Corruption in the Philippines,' which reported a February 2000 Social Weather Stations survey finding that 62 percent of respondents believed there were significant levels of corruption in the judiciary, 65 percent that many or most lawyers could be bribed and 57 percent the same of judges, alongside accusations of deliberate delay, incompetence, arrogance, neglect of duty, partiality and immorality. He offered two assurances: that while there are some undesirable judges and lawyers the vast majority are honest, competent, hardworking and God-fearing, and that the Supreme Court had instituted a wide-ranging reform program. He described the 'Davide Watch' announced on November 30, 1998 and its day-to-day Action Program for Judicial Reform, supported by the national government, local donors, UNDP, the World Bank, ADB, UNICEF, the Asia Foundation and several bilateral donors, and covering law-school curricula, the bar examinations, aid to poor students, screening of appointees, continuing legal education and performance monitoring. Its central theme, he said, was a clarion call to ethics: the Court enforced the Code of Judicial Conduct and the Code of Professional Responsibility more strictly than RA 6713 required of officials generally, and for the first time in its 100-year history had censured one of its own members, dismissed a Court of Appeals justice, suspended the Sandiganbayan presiding magistrate, and disrobed, fined or disciplined hundreds of lower-court judges. But discipline was not enough. With more than a third of trial courts vacant and judges paid less than some Makati clerks, he argued that compensation had to be rationalized through real fiscal independence -- a lump-sum appropriation of about two percent of the national budget -- and exemption from the Salary Standardization Law, while rejecting both LGU allowances and a corporate fundraising offer as threats to independence. He closed on the four 'ins' of a good judge: integrity, independence, intelligence and industry.
